title: It came from different places, but money talked in House races
summary: Tens of millions of dollars flowed into Maryland's House races this year, from PACs to small donors to well-heeled candidates themselves, and it made the difference in the outcomes, with one notable exception. And even there, money was a notable factor.
content:
by Will Hammann, Maryland Matters July 17, 2026

by Will Hammann, Maryland Matters July 17, 2026

Tens of millions of dollars flowed into Maryland’s congressional primary races this year, from small grass-roots donors to political action committees to some well-heeled candidates themselves, and that money made the difference in the outcomes — with one notable exception.

Even in that race, money was hardly a negligible factor: Rep. April McClain Delaney (D-6th) loaned her campaign $11 million in a successful bid to beat back a challenge from David Trone, a billionaire former member of Congress who loaned himself $25 million.

“We don’t usually see a race where there are two who can self-finance to that extent,” said David Karol, associate professor of government and politics at the University of Maryland. “It was no David versus Goliath story here. I mean, it was the centimillionaire versus the billionaire, there’s no little guy in that story.”

The numbers come from the candidates’ second-quarter filings Wednesday with the Federal Election Commission.

Besides the Trone-McClain Delaney match, the reports showed the full range of funding sources for candidates in the crowded 5th District Democratic primary.

Quincy Bareebe loaned herself more than $6.6 million of the $6.8 million she raised. Harry Dunn raised $4.9 million, of which $4 million came from small, individual donors. And Adrian Boafo, the eventual winner of the race, raised $1.7 million — but benefited from more than $11 million in PAC spending on his behalf.

Public financing programs faced biggest year yet in county executive primaries

The influx of money to Boafo’s campaign began with $500,000 from AmeriPAC, the political action committee headed by outgoing Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-5th), who endorsed Boafo out of the field of 24 Democratic hopefuls. That was followed by millions in independent expenditures from groups like crypto super PAC Protect Progress and the AIPAC-affiliated United Democracy Project, along with endorsements from leading Democrats like Gov. Wes Moore and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks.

The outside spending drew the ire of Boafo’s opponents, including Bareebe, Dunn and former Prince George’s County Executive Rushern Baker who issued a joint statement calling on Boafo to publicly disavow the PAC support.

“How do you have somebody supporting Adrian Boafo, but also supporting MAGA Republicans?” Dunn asked of PACs and their affiliates, who support candidates on both sides of the aisle.

It’s not the first time that Dunn, a former U.S. Capitol Police officer who was at the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, has raised more in individual donations but lost to a candidate who was boosted by PAC funding.

In 2024, Dunn raised just over $6 million, of which $4.4 million came from small, individual donors for a race in the 3rd House District. But he lost to Sarah Elfreth, who raised $2.3 million but was the beneficiary of independent spending from groups like AIPAC.

The influx of large donors is a reaction to the success of small donor-funded campaigns, according to Dunn.

“They’re like, ‘Oh s—, we’ve got to buy this election now’ … I think it’s a cause and effect,” he said. “Because they knew that I’m not a person that’s going to listen to special interests, and that I’m always going to be a voice of the people and not them.”

Karol said technology has allowed candidates like Dunn to raise so heavily from small donors across the country. Donors can now contribute online where they used to have to find a candidate’s address and mail in their donations. Convincing people to do so through direct mail was expensive for campaigns, he said.

Even in 1992, former California Gov. Jerry Brown tried to make reliance on small donors a selling point in his own presidential bid. “He said, call my 1-800 number. Operators are standing by. And you would have to give your credit card number,” Karol recalled.

Karol also noted that small donors angry at high-profile candidates of their opposite party often donate to congressional races around the country, like in 2018 when former Rep. Beto O’Rourke’s 2018 tried to unseat Republican Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas)

“Democratic donors hated Ted Cruz, so they gave [O’Rourke] a huge amount of money when this was a longshot race,” one O’Rourke lost by less than 3%.

As of June 3, Dunn received a total of $667,216 large individual donations from all 50 states – $49,219 from within Maryland, and a combined $199,281 from California, Florida and New York.

Of Boafo’s more than $1 million in such donations, $215,063 came from Maryland. From the three states besides Maryland that topped Dunn’s list, Boafo received $401,970, and the rest came from more than 30 other states.

As Boafo moves onto the general election against Chris Chaffee, now a two-time Republican nominee for the district, Dunn said he doesn’t have a desire to run for office again.

“But I do have a desire to keep standing up for the people, and the people need somebody. Whether you have a title in front of your name, or before or after your name, they don’t care,” he said. “They just want somebody to actually stand up for them, and I’ll always do that no matter what.”
